title: Pot de Crème au Chocolat
subtitle: Baked chocolate cream in little pots
excerpt: A rich baked chocolate custard, denser than mousse and silkier than ganache, served in individual pots or ramekins. Set by egg yolks and cream with no gelatine, and baked in a bain-marie until barely trembling.
sourceNotes: Pot de crème is a classical French baked custard, made in the small lidded pots (pots à crème) that give it its name. The chocolate version is the most popular. Auguste Escoffier, Le Guide Culinaire (1903), establishes the method. Julia Child, Mastering the Art of French Cooking (1961), gives the home version. The texture of a well-made pot de crème is somewhere between a very firm mousse and a very soft ganache, barely set, completely smooth, deeply flavoured.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Must be made at least 3 hours ahead and can be made the day before. Keep refrigerated and covered. Remove from the fridge 15 minutes before serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: The technique of gradually raising the temperature of a cold or room-temperature ingredient (such as egg yolks) by adding small amounts of a hot liquid before combining them fully. Tempering prevents the eggs from scrambling when they meet the hot cream. A ladle of hot cream stirred into the beaten yolks before adding the rest is the standard method.

content.text: A pot de crème is a baked custard: egg yolks combined with hot cream, poured into small pots, and baked in a bain-marie at a very low temperature until just trembling. The chocolate version uses dark chocolate melted into the cream. The critical step is
the egg yolks, adding the hot cream gradually so they warm up without scrambling. From this point the method is extremely simple.
Heat the oven to 160°C fan. Boil a full kettle. Place the chopped chocolate in a large heatproof bowl.
Bring the cream and milk to a simmer in the saucepan. Pour over the chocolate and leave for 1 minute, then stir until smooth. Add the vanilla and a pinch of salt.
In a bowl, whisk the egg yolks with the sugar until pale. Slowly pour the warm chocolate cream into the yolks, whisking constantly (tempering). The mixture should be smooth and pourable.
Strain through a fine sieve to remove any bits of cooked egg. Divide among 6 ramekins. Set the ramekins in the roasting tin and pour boiling water to come halfway up the sides.

Bake for 25 to 30 minutes. The custards are done when the edges are set and the centre still wobbles when shaken. Remove from the water bath and cool completely, then refrigerate for at least 3 hours. Serve cold, with a little whipped cream if liked.

items.symptom: The custard has a grainy or curdled texture
items.cause: The egg yolks were added to cream that was too hot, or the bain-marie temperature was too high.
items.fix: Temper the yolks carefully by adding the hot cream in a slow stream while whisking. Keep the bain-marie water at a simmer, not a boil. The maximum internal temperature of a successful custard is about 82°C.

items.symptom: The custard is liquid after baking
items.cause: Not enough baking time, or the oven was too cool.
items.fix: Return to the bain-marie and bake for a further 5 to 10 minutes. The custard should wobble at the centre but the edges should be set. The custard will continue to firm as it chills.

items.symptom: The surface is bubbly rather than smooth
items.cause: Air was whisked into the custard, or the temperature was too high.
items.fix: Strain through a fine sieve before filling the ramekins. Pop any surface bubbles with the tip of a cocktail stick before placing in the oven.

content.text: Pot de crème is a dessert of the French restaurant tradition. It has appeared on Parisian menus for at least two centuries. The appeal is its simplicity: it needs no special technique beyond making a custard, and it rewards good chocolate. The small lidded pots (pots à crème) in which it is baked and served are their own category of French kitchenware, sold in specialist shops across France.
